title: House Robber II
description: Brute force to optimized: direct circular-state recursion versus two linear House Robber runs excluding one end each.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Houses are arranged in a CIRCLE (the first and last houses are also considered adjacent). Given the money in each house, return the maximum amount robbable without robbing two adjacent houses.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums array, arranged in a circle"],["Output","Maximum sum achievable with no two circularly-adjacent elements chosen"],["Key Insight","The first and last house cannot BOTH be robbed, so the answer is the better of two LINEAR House Robber runs, each excluding one of them"],["Constraints","Up to 100 houses"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Houses in a circle, first and last are also adjacent\"","Split the circular constraint into two simpler LINEAR sub-problems: one excluding the first house, one excluding the last house, since at most one of them can ever be robbed"]]}

blocks.text: The only real difference from the plain (linear) House Robber problem is that the first and last houses are now ALSO considered adjacent, meaning they cannot BOTH be robbed. This single additional constraint can be handled by running the ORIGINAL linear House Robber algorithm twice: once on the array EXCLUDING the last house, and once EXCLUDING the first house, then taking the better of the two results, since at least one of the two houses must be excluded from consideration in any valid answer.

blocks.title: Analogy: Robbing Houses Arranged Around a Circular Driveway
blocks.text: Picture houses arranged around a circular driveway, where the very first and very last house are also next-door neighbors. Since these two special neighbors can never BOTH be robbed, considering two separate straight-line scenarios (excluding one house or the other) covers every valid possibility.

blocks.caption: Run the linear House Robber twice, excluding the first house in one run and the last house in the other

blocks.text: Maximum = 3 (rob only the middle house, since the first and last are circularly adjacent to each other and would conflict).
Maximum = 4 (rob houses at positions 0 and 2, values 1 and 3, excluding the last house from consideration).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In any valid robbery plan, EITHER the first house is robbed, OR it is not; the same applies to the last house, and they cannot BOTH be robbed since they are circularly adjacent.

Observation 2: If the last house is definitely NOT robbed, the problem reduces exactly to the plain linear House Robber problem on the array WITHOUT its last element.

Observation 3: Symmetrically, if the first house is definitely NOT robbed, the problem reduces to the plain linear House Robber problem on the array WITHOUT its first element.

Observation 4: Since every valid plan falls into at least one of these two cases (first not robbed, or last not robbed), the true answer is simply the BETTER of running the plain linear algorithm on these two overlapping slices.
This leads to reusing the plain linear House Robber algorithm twice, on two slightly different slices of the array, taking the better result.
Recursively try robbing or skipping each house in the circular arrangement directly, tracking whether the FIRST house was robbed to correctly enforce the circular adjacency constraint at the end.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Directly tracking the circular constraint through recursion handles it correctly but requires extra state.

This is both more complex to implement AND still exponential without memoization; splitting into two linear sub-problems is both simpler and directly efficient by reusing the already-known linear solution.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential without memoization.
Space: O(n) recursion depth, plus extra state tracking.
Limitation: splitting the circular problem into two independent LINEAR sub-problems avoids the need for extra state tracking entirely, directly reusing the efficient linear algorithm.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Handle the trivial case of exactly one house directly (rob it, since there is no circular conflict with itself). Otherwise, run the plain linear House Robber algorithm (two rolling variables) on the array EXCLUDING the last house, then again on the array EXCLUDING the first house, and return the LARGER of the two results.
Reuse the plain linear House Robber algorithm twice, on two overlapping slices excluding the first or last house respectively.

blocks.text: Since the first and last houses can never BOTH be robbed (due to circular adjacency), any valid optimal plan must exclude at least one of them entirely from consideration; running the well-understood LINEAR House Robber algorithm on the slice excluding the last house covers every plan where the last house is never robbed, and running it on the slice excluding the first house covers every plan where the first house is never robbed, together covering every possible valid plan, so taking the better of the two results is guaranteed correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), two linear passes.
Space: O(1) extra (or O(n) if slices are physically copied).

blocks.text: House Robber II is a clean example of reducing a more complex CIRCULAR constraint into two simpler, already-solved LINEAR sub-problems, rather than modifying the core algorithm directly.

items: Forgetting the special case of exactly one house (where there is no actual circular conflict, since a house cannot be adjacent to itself).
Attempting to directly modify the linear algorithm to handle circularity instead of the simpler reduction to two linear sub-problems.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "reduce the circular problem to two linear sub-problems, since the first and last house can never both be robbed" demonstrates a valuable general problem-reduction skill.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "the first and last elements are also considered adjacent (circular)", think: solve it as two overlapping linear sub-problems, excluding one end in each.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The direct circular-recursion approach is both complex and exponential without memoization; the two-linear-runs approach costs O(n), the standard efficient and elegant solution.

items: Pattern: reducing a circular constraint into two overlapping linear sub-problems.
Core Idea: the first and last houses can never both be robbed, so run linear House Robber twice, excluding one end each time.
Time: exponential for the direct circular-recursion approach, O(n) for the two-linear-runs approach.
Space: O(n) recursion depth plus extra state for the direct approach, O(1) extra for the two-linear-runs approach.
Most Important Observation: a circular constraint often reduces cleanly to a small number of linear sub-problems.
Interview Difficulty: a clean, moderately easy DP variant once the reduction is spotted.
One line memory trick: exclude the first, or exclude the last, take the better.
